title: Accounting Concepts: Meaning and the Going Concern Concept
summary: What accounting concepts are, why we need them, and the going concern concept with its effect on assets, expenses and liabilities.

p: Accounting concepts are the basic assumptions, rules and principles that guide how financial information is recorded and presented. They are also called accounting assumptions or accounting principles.
Purpose: to make accounting uniform; to make accounts comparable; to make financial statements reliable; to guide accountants when they must decide; and to give a framework for accounting practice.
The going concern concept assumes that the business will continue to operate for the foreseeable future and has no plan to close down or to cut down its activities greatly.

Effect on assets: assets are recorded at cost, not at selling price; depreciation is worked out over the useful life of the asset; there is no need to value assets as if the business were being sold. Example: a machine bought for ₦100,000 is recorded at ₦100,000, not at what it could be sold for today.

Effect on revenue and expenses: they are matched over accounting periods and the long-term view is taken; prepayments and accruals are recognised. Example: rent paid for three years in advance is spread over the three years.

Effect on liabilities: long-term liabilities are treated as long term, and the business does not have to pay all its debts at once. Example: a ten-year loan is not shown as a current (short-term) liability.

sections.h: When going concern does NOT apply
p: The concept does not apply when the business is bankrupt, is closing down, is being liquidated (wound up) or is in severe financial difficulty. Then assets are valued at their break-up value, which is what they can be sold for.

ABC Company bought equipment for ₦500,000 with a life of 5 years. If going concern applies, the equipment is recorded at ₦500,000, depreciation is ₦100,000 a year (₦500,000 ÷ 5) and the balance sheet shows a falling value year by year. If the company is closing down and the equipment can be sold for only ₦200,000, the equipment is valued at ₦200,000 and an immediate loss of ₦300,000 is shown.

title: Accrual and Materiality Concepts
summary: Matching revenue and expenses to the right period, prepayments and accruals, cash basis compared with accrual basis, and the materiality concept.

p: The accrual concept says that revenue and expenses must be recognised when they are earned or incurred, not when cash is received or paid. It is also called the matching concept: expenses are matched with the revenue they help to earn in the same period.
Revenue is recognised when goods are delivered or services are done, not necessarily when payment is received. Example: goods sold in December and paid for in January are recorded as a December sale.
An expense is recognised when it is incurred, in the period in which the benefit is received. Example: electricity used in December but paid for in January is a December expense.
A prepayment is a payment made in advance. It is treated as an asset until the period it covers. Example: ₦12,000 rent paid in January for one year gives ₦1,000 of expense each month.
An accrual is an expense that has been incurred but is not yet paid. It is shown as a liability. Example: December salaries paid in January belong to December's accounts.

On the cash basis, we record only when cash changes hands. On the accrual basis, we record when the amount is earned or incurred. The accrual basis gives a truer profit, an accurate financial position, comparable periods and better decisions.
Worked example, December 2023. Sales ₦300,000 (₦200,000 cash and ₦100,000 on credit). Expenses ₦150,000 (₦100,000 paid and ₦50,000 still owing).

The materiality concept says that only items big enough to affect decisions need to be shown separately. Small, unimportant items can be grouped together or treated simply. Do not waste time on trivial things; focus on what matters.

Whether an item is material depends on its size (compared with profit or total assets), its nature, and the business. A guide: an item is usually material if leaving it out or showing it wrongly would change a user's decision, or if it is more than about 5 to 10 per cent of profit. Some items are material whatever the size, such as fraud.

Material items: a ₦1,000,000 expense in a small business; any fraud; a large bad debt; a major lawsuit; a change in accounting policy. Immaterial items: a ₦500 expense in a large company; small office supplies; minor repairs; a tiny petty cash shortage.

Examples: a ₦1,000 stapler is recorded as an expense, not as an asset, because it is not worth depreciating over five years. A ₦2,000,000 delivery van is an asset and is depreciated. A company with an annual profit of ₦10,000,000 has stationery of ₦5,000 (0.05% of profit, immaterial) and a bad debt of ₦800,000 (8% of profit, material and should be shown separately).

title: Consistency and Dual Aspect Concepts
summary: Using the same methods year after year, when methods may change, and the dual aspect concept with the accounting equation.

p: Once an accounting method has been chosen, it should be used in the same way from one period to the next unless there is a good reason to change. Purpose: to make accounts comparable over time; to stop people from manipulating profits; to keep the accounts reliable; and to allow trends to be studied.

Areas that need consistency: the depreciation method (if vans are depreciated by the straight-line method, keep doing so); stock valuation (if you use FIFO, first in first out, keep using it); and other policies such as how revenue is recognised, the percentage for bad debts and what is treated as an asset.

Acceptable reasons to change: a change in accounting standards; a new method that gives a fairer picture; a change in the nature of the business; or a legal requirement. When a method is changed, the change must be disclosed, the effect stated, the reason given and earlier figures may need to be adjusted.

A machine costs ₦500,000. In Year 1, straight-line depreciation at 10% gives ₦50,000. If the owner switches in Year 2 to reducing balance at 20%, the charge is 20% of ₦450,000 (cost less Year 1 depreciation), which is ₦90,000. Profit in Year 2 falls only because of the new method, so the two years cannot be fairly compared. The right approach is to keep the same method unless there is a justified reason to change. (Your notes show ₦50,000 and ₦80,000; the working above is the correct arithmetic for the reducing balance method.)

The dual aspect concept says that every transaction has two aspects, a debit and a credit, and these are always equal. It is the foundation of the double entry system. The basic equation is Assets = Capital + Liabilities, and it must always balance. In other words, what the business owns equals what the business owes (to the owner and to others).
Transaction 1: started business with ₦100,000 cash. Cash (asset) increases by ₦100,000 (debit) and capital increases by ₦100,000 (credit). Assets ₦100,000 = Capital ₦100,000.
Transaction 2: bought goods for ₦30,000 cash. Purchases (an expense) ₦30,000 is debited and cash falls by ₦30,000 (credit). Assets ₦70,000 = Capital ₦100,000 less the expense ₦30,000.

Transaction 3: bought furniture ₦50,000 on credit. Furniture (asset) rises by ₦50,000 (debit) and the creditor (liability) rises by ₦50,000 (credit). Assets ₦70,000 + ₦50,000 = ₦120,000, which equals capital ₦100,000 + liability ₦50,000 less the expense ₦30,000 = ₦120,000.
Benefits: it lets us check accuracy by a trial balance; it gives a complete record; it shows where funds come from and how they are used; and it is the basis of the financial statements.

title: The Prudence Concept and Applying All the Concepts
summary: Being careful about profits and losses, how prudence affects stock, debtors and assets, a summary table of the six concepts and a worked example applying them.

p: The prudence concept says that when in doubt, choose the option that is less likely to overstate assets or income. Its motto is: 'Anticipate no profits, but provide for all possible losses.'

Revenue: do not count it until it is reasonably certain; do not record a profit on goods not yet sold, even if you expect a high price. Expenses: record them as soon as possible and provide for likely losses; it is better to overstate expenses than to understate them. Assets: do not overvalue them; write down if the value falls, and do not write up if the value rises. Liabilities: do not understate them; provide for probable liabilities.
An asset that cost ₦100,000 but is now worth ₦80,000 is written down to ₦80,000. If it is now worth ₦120,000, it stays at ₦100,000.

Stock valuation: stock is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value (NRV, the selling price less selling costs). Stock cost ₦50,000 and worth ₦45,000: record ₦45,000. Stock cost ₦50,000 and worth ₦60,000: record ₦50,000. (Your notes say 'market value'; the accounting standard uses net realisable value.)
Provision for doubtful debts: debtors ₦100,000, and 5% may not pay, so provide ₦5,000. This reduces profit now instead of later.
Depreciation: charge depreciation even on an asset that is not being used.
Contingent liabilities: possible losses, such as a lawsuit not yet decided, should be disclosed or provided for.

Do not be too prudent. Do not deliberately understate profit. Aim for a fair presentation. Prudence means provide for an expected loss of ₦10,000. Optimism (wrong) would record an expected profit of ₦10,000 before it is earned.

title: The General Journal: Meaning, Format and Uses
summary: What the general journal is, its columns, how to write an entry and nine situations in which it is used.

p: The general journal is a book of original (prime) entry used to record transactions that cannot be recorded in the other specialised books. It is also called the journal proper or just the journal. A journal is a record, in order of date, of business transactions showing the accounts to be debited and credited, the amounts and an explanation (the narration).
The journal has five columns.

head: Column
What is written
rows: The date of the transaction (day, month, year)
The account to debit (written first, at the left), the account to credit (written below, indented), and the narration in brackets
The ledger page number, filled in when the entry is posted
The amount to debit, on the same line as the debit account
The amount to credit, on the same line as the credit account

p: The debit account is written first, at the left. The credit account is written below it and moved in. The narration, which starts with 'Being' and explains the transaction, is written in brackets. Total debits must equal total credits.

1. Opening entries: recording assets, liabilities and capital when a business begins or when books are opened. 2. Closing entries: transferring revenue and expense accounts to the profit and loss account at the end of the period. 3. Purchase of assets on credit: for example machinery bought from a supplier on credit. 4. Sale of assets on credit: for example selling old furniture on credit. 5. Correction of errors. 6. Adjustments: bad debts, provision for depreciation, accruals and prepayments. 7. Transfer entries: moving an amount from one account to another, such as goods taken for personal use. 8. Writing off bad debts. 9. Any other entry that does not belong in a specialised book.

Purchases of goods for resale on credit go into the purchases journal (and credit sales into the sales journal). Only purchases or sales of assets such as machinery and furniture, which are not goods for resale, go through the general journal.

title: The Analytical Cash Book: Meaning and Format
summary: What an analytical cash book is, why it is called analytical, its format, columns and features.

p: An analytical cash book is a cash book with extra columns that split receipts and payments according to their nature or purpose. It is also called a columnar or multi-column cash book. It is 'analytical' because it analyses (breaks down) each amount into its type.
Purpose: to analyse cash and bank transactions; to show different types of receipts and payments separately; to give more detailed information; and to help in budget control.
Analysis can be by source of income (sales, rent, commission), by type of expense (purchases, wages, rent), by department or project, or by customer or supplier.
Receipts side (debit, left): Date, Details, Folio, Total, Sales, Debtors, Other income. Payments side (credit, right): Date, Details, Folio, Total, Purchases, Wages, Rent, Sundry.

The number and names of analysis columns depend on the needs of the business. Common receipts columns are sales, debtors, capital and other income. Common payments columns are purchases, salaries, rent and creditors.
1. The total column shows the whole amount received or paid. It is the sum of the analysis columns for each entry and is the one used for balancing.
2. The analysis columns break the total down by category.
3. The sundry (or other) column is for odd items that do not fit the other columns, such as small or rare transactions.
4. The balance is worked out from the total column only, never from the analysis columns.
Every entry goes in the total column. The same amount goes in only ONE analysis column. For each entry, the total equals the amount in the analysis column. Only the total column is balanced.

title: Preparing and Posting the Analytical Cash Book
summary: A complete worked example for January 2024, verifying the balance, the advantages, and how to post the analysis columns to the ledger.

p: 1. Decide which analysis columns are needed. 2. Write the date and details. 3. Enter the total amount in the total column. 4. Enter the same amount in the right analysis column. 5. At the end of the period, total all columns and balance using the total column only.

Jan 1: cash balance ₦50,000. Jan 2: cash sales ₦20,000. Jan 5: received from debtor John ₦15,000. Jan 8: paid for purchases ₦25,000. Jan 10: paid wages ₦8,000. Jan 12: cash sales ₦18,000. Jan 15: paid rent ₦10,000. Jan 18: received commission ₦5,000. Jan 20: paid creditor Ade ₦12,000. Jan 25: paid electricity ₦3,000. Jan 28: cash sales ₦22,000. Jan 30: paid salaries ₦15,000.
Receipts side (debit):
The wages column holds both wages and salaries because they are the same kind of expense (staff pay). The balance c/d is the difference between the two totals.

Receipts side total ₦130,000 (the opening balance ₦50,000 plus receipts ₦80,000). Payments made ₦73,000 (25,000 + 8,000 + 10,000 + 12,000 + 3,000 + 15,000). Closing balance = 130,000 less 73,000 = ₦57,000. The analysis columns of each side also agree: receipts 60,000 + 15,000 + 5,000 = ₦80,000; payments 25,000 + 23,000 + 10,000 + 12,000 + 3,000 = ₦73,000.

It gives detailed information; it saves time because analysis is done while recording; it helps decisions by showing spending patterns; it makes posting easier because only the column totals are posted; it gives better control over spending; and it is quick to find and total any category.

The cash account itself is the cash book, so the total column needs no separate posting. From the receipts analysis columns, post a CREDIT to each account: Sales account ₦60,000; Debtors (or John's account) ₦15,000; Commission account ₦5,000. From the payments analysis columns, post a DEBIT to each account: Purchases ₦25,000; Wages ₦23,000; Rent ₦10,000; Creditors (or Ade's account) ₦12,000. Items in the sundry column are posted one by one (here Electricity ₦3,000).
Remember that the debtor and creditor columns are posted to the individual accounts of each person, in the personal ledgers.
